t.1.39.1: If you are able to cure anything that has been bitten by me here, then, Kāśyapa, bring back to life this tree that I have bitten.
t.1.39.2: Whatever supreme power of mantras you possess, display it and exert yourself. I shall burn this banyan tree while you look on, O best of the twice-born.
t.1.39.3: Kāśyapa said: Bite, O lord of snakes, this tree that you have in mind; O serpent, I shall bring it back to life after it has been bitten by you.
t.1.39.4: The bard said: Thus addressed by the great-souled Kāśyapa, that lord of the Nāgas, the foremost of serpents, approached a tree, a banyan, and bit it.
t.1.39.5: That tree, O greatly splendid one, being bitten by him, was at once filled with the venom of the serpent and blazed up on all sides.
t.1.39.6: Having burned that tree, the Nāga spoke again to Kāśyapa: "Make an effort, best of the twice-born, and bring this lord of the forest back to life!"
t.1.39.7: Then, gathering up all the ash of the tree that had been reduced to ashes by the fiery power of the lord of serpents, Kāśyapa spoke these words.
t.1.39.8: O lord of serpents, behold the power of my knowledge on this tree; I shall bring it back to life while you look on, O serpent.
t.1.39.9: Then the blessed and learned Kāśyapa, best of the twice-born, by his knowledge brought back to life the tree that had been reduced to a heap of ashes.
t.1.39.10: He made it a sprout, then one bearing a pair of leaves, then leafy and branching, and then once more a tree with spreading boughs.
t.1.39.11: Seeing that tree brought back to life by the great-souled Kāśyapa, Takṣaka said, "O Brahmin, this is most wondrous in you."
t.1.39.13: Whatever reward you desire to obtain from that best of kings, that very thing I myself shall give to you, even if it is hard to obtain.
t.1.39.12: O lord of brahmins, granting that you could destroy the poison of me or of one like me, what gain are you seeking in going there, O ascetic rich in austerities?
t.1.39.15: Then your blazing fame, renowned throughout the three worlds, would vanish from here like the sun stripped of its rays.
t.1.39.14: Since the lord of men has been overpowered by a Brahmin's curse and his life is spent, your success, O Brahmin, however hard you strive, would be doubtful.
t.1.39.17: Whatever wealth you seek from that king, I will give you more than that today; turn back, O best of the twice-born.
t.1.39.16: I am going there in search of wealth; be willing to give that to me, O serpent, and then I shall turn back home, O best of serpents.
t.1.39.18: Having heard the words of Takṣaka, Kāśyapa, best of the twice-born, wise and of very great splendor, reflected deeply concerning the king.
t.1.39.19: Then the radiant Kāśyapa, possessed of divine knowledge, knowing that the king, the descendant of Pāṇḍu, had reached the end of his life, turned back, that best of sages, having received from Takṣaka as much wealth as he desired.
t.1.39.20: When that great-souled Kāśyapa had turned back by agreement, Takṣaka went swiftly to the city named after the elephant.
t.1.39.21: Then, as he was going, Takṣaka heard that the lord of the earth was being carefully guarded by poison-removing spells and antidotes.
t.1.39.22: Then the king pondered: "He must be deceived by me through the use of magic; what means might there be?"
t.1.39.23: Then the serpent Takṣaka sent forth snakes in the guise of ascetics, bearing fruits, leaves and water, to the king.
t.1.39.25: Sūta said: Thus instructed by Takṣaka, those serpents did as they were told; they brought to the king darbha grass, water, and fruits.
t.1.39.24: Go to the king, all of you, unperturbed, as though on some business, ostensibly to have the king accept an offering of fruits, leaves and water.
t.1.39.26: And that mighty lord of kings accepted it all; and having done what was needed for them, he said to them, "You may go."
t.1.39.27: When those Nāgas, who had taken on the guise of ascetics, had departed, that lord of men spoke to his ministers and his friends.
t.1.39.28: Let your honors, together with me, eat all of these sweet fruits that have been brought by the ascetics.
t.1.39.29: Then the king, together with his ministers, wished to take the fruits; in the fruit that was taken up by the king there appeared a tiny worm, very small, black-eyed and coppery in colour, O Śaunaka.
t.1.39.30: Taking hold of it, that best of kings said this to his ministers: "The sun is going to its setting; today I have no fear of poison."
t.1.39.32: And the ministers, driven by Time, followed him in this. Having spoken thus, that king of kings placed the little worm upon his neck and laughed at once, about to die, his senses lost.
t.1.39.31: Let that sage be true of speech: let this worm bite me, having become the one named Takṣaka, and so the curse would be warded off.
t.1.39.33: And even as he was laughing, he was encircled by Takṣaka with his coils, Takṣaka having emerged from that fruit which had been presented to the king.
